chunks: "An EMI shield is a conductive enclosure or barrier that goes around a circuit, or sits between two circuits, to stop electromagnetic energy from getting in or out.

On a PCB it's usually a stamped metal can, often tin-plated steel or nickel silver, soldered to a ground fence of pads on the board, sometimes with a separate frame and a snap-on lid so you can get at the parts underneath.
At the system level it's a metal or metallised-plastic enclosure with gaskets, and for cables it's the braid or foil shield.

I'd use one when layout can't do the job: an RF transmitter or receiver section, so it neither radiates nor picks up noise; a noisy source like a switching regulator, clock generator or processor I can't change; very sensitive analog like a microvolt sensor front end; or when a product fails radiated emissions or has desense and I need a quick targeted fix.
The cost side is real: the can adds BOM and assembly cost, height and heat trapping, makes rework and probing harder, and it leaks at seams and openings.
So I treat it as a last resort, but I reserve footprint space for it at layout time so it can be added without a respin."
